title: SDK integration lab: auth, env, and Optimize playground
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood SDK quickstart in Python and TypeScript, environment variables and secret management, demo of Console and Optimize suggestions, discussion of private VPC deployment constraints and security requirements. Agreed to run a small pilot with a sandbox project and exchange security docs.
action_items: Sofia - Share quickstart repo and short how-to by 2025-09-19
Ethan - Provide sample docker-compose and env examples and a minimal benchmark script by 2025-09-22
Maya - Confirm pilot scope (2 endpoints, 1 team) and internal stakeholders by 2025-09-23
Liam - Send list of security questions and SOC 2 evidence requests by 2025-09-20
next_steps: Redwood to provision sandbox API key scoped to dev-only env
Customer to attempt Python quickstart and log issues in the shared repo
Schedule pilot kickoff next week (Sofia to propose times)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Clearview Eng Manager), Noah Kim (Backend), Liam O'Connor (Security)
Links referenced: Quickstart repo https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstarts (shared), Deck: https://rbwd.co/poc-deck, Security checklist stub https://rbwd.co/sec-check

[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um we're going to run through a very hands-on lab today, sdk quickstart in python and typescript, auth patterns and then dig into the Console Optimize suggestions — please chime in with questions.
[00:12] Maya: thanks, excited. quick background — our team is building a clinical summarization feature, low latency, PII must stay in region, and IT requires SSO + keys in vault.
[00:25] Sofia: got it. that's helpful. ethan will lead the code walkthrough and then we'll show the console optimize tab and how batching/cache helps cost.
[00:33] Ethan: cool, I'll share my screen, uh quick note — my terminal font is small so say if you can't read it. first step is python sdk pip install redwood-sdk, but we also have a TS example via npm i @redwood/inference.
[00:47] [01:02] Ethan: here's the minimal python snippet -- import redwood, client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) , response = client.generate("Summarize the note...") 
[01:18] Noah: quick question — we use Hashi Vault, do you have a recommended pattern for storing the API key? we can't put keys in plain env on prod.
[01:26] Ethan: yep, common pattern is to inject at runtime from Vault into the container's env. we also support short-lived tokens via our auth broker if you want a federated flow — although the broker needs network access to your IDP.
[01:40] Liam: for security review — does Redwood support customer-managed KMS for data at rest on private? and is the key rotation visible in audit logs?
[01:48] Sofia: short answer: yes for private deployments we integrate with customer KMS and rotation events are surfaced in audit. we'll send the SOC 2 and encryption docs after call — Ethan has the links.
[02:05] Ethan: nav to Console > Projects > Optimize tab — here you'll see suggested batching and cache rules after a short profiling run. for example, we suggested a 32-token batching window on your sample workload which saved about 22% token cost in our sandbox.
[02:22] Maya: how invasive is the SDK change for us? we have a microservice in Go and a node.js api gateway.
[02:30] Ethan: SDKs are thin wrappers — the node sdk mirrors the python calls, and for go we'd recommend calling our HTTP endpoint through a tiny client. main changes are around caching prefixes and adding the session K-V cache handling on the api gateway if you want fast completion times.
[02:48] [05:05] Ethan: (typing) i'll show the ts example now — const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, env: process.env.REDWOOD_ENV || 'sandbox' }); client.chat.completions.create...
[05:20] Noah: will the env variable for REDWOOD_ENV map to a VPC endpoint if we point it to private? we want traffic to stay on our peered network.
[05:29] Ethan: yes, if you provision a Private endpoint we give you a private hostname; the SDK simply hits that host when REDWOOD_ENV is set to your private tag. small caveat: if you're on-prem with no DNS peering, you'll need a route to the private net.
[05:44] Maya: do you have an example docker-compose or k8s manifest for injecting vault secrets?
[05:51] Ethan: yes — I uploaded a small docker-compose to the quickstart repo. it uses envsubst to inject VAULT_TOKEN at container start. it's minimal — for prod we'd recommend an init sidecar that fetches secrets.
[06:08] Liam: a couple of gotchas from our security playbook: we need RBAC for token issuance, audit trail retention for 13 months, and per-team model access controls. can Redwood do per-route RBAC?
[06:18] Sofia: yes, per-route RBAC is supported in the Console through token scopes and route-level permissions. retention windows are configurable for enterprise plans. we'll include the admin role matrix in the follow-up.
[06:31] [10:00] Ethan: moving on — Optimize's profile run. i'll run a short workload now against the sandbox key so you can see the suggestions live.
[10:15] (background typing and short pause)
[10:30] Ethan: ok results are in. Optimize suggests: enable prefix KV cache for similarity prompts, set max_batch_size to 8 for the current qps, and enable 4-bit quantized variant for dev to save cost.
[10:44] Noah: 4-bit sounds risky for quality. any quality delta we should worry about?
[10:50] Ethan: there's usually a small delta in rare tokens — we instrument regressions using your eval set, and Optimize can flag regressions automatically. for a high-precision clinical workflow, we recommend canary the quantized model on a subset and run the eval harness.
[11:08] Maya: can that eval harness run on our CI? we want to gate deployment.
[11:12] Ethan: yep, we provide a cli tool you can point at a prompt set — it returns pass/fail and a regression report. link in repo.
[11:18] [15:40] Maya: about latency — our SLO is p95 under 400ms for short notes. is that feasible on hosted or do we need Dedicated?
[15:48] Ethan: depends on volume. for small qps (<20 qps) hosted with proper batching and KV cache should hit p95 <400ms for short sequences. if you push higher throughput or require lower jitter, Dedicated reserved GPU pools are recommended.
[16:02] Liam: and what about graceful degradation? if the region hits capacity, will requests fail open or fallback to another model?
[16:10] Sofia: we route by policy — you can set fallback to a smaller model or another region; we also have automatic throttle and queueing policies. that said cross-region fallbacks may have data residency implications.
[16:25] Noah: any idea of per-request cost with caching vs no cache?
[16:29] Ethan: ballpark — with prefix caching active we saw token costs drop around 30% on the demo dataset. actual savings depend on repetition in your prompts. Optimize provides per-token cost breakdown in Console.
[16:45] [20:00] (short demo where Ethan runs the python quickstart live)
[20:10] Ethan: i ran the python quickstart, you can see the request id in the console logs — request: rdw-req-4567, it shows token usage, latency, and which kernel variant served it.
[20:22] Maya: the console logs look useful. can we stream logs to our Splunk/SIEM?
[20:29] Sofia: yes, we support log export via S3 + Kinesis or direct ingestion into common SIEMs. we'll put the ingestion templates in the follow-up.
[20:41] Liam: also need to validate network egress for healthcare regulator — any outbound domains list?
[20:47] Ethan: yes, we'll provide the full list of hostnames and ranges. note for private deployments your egress is internal only.
[21:05] [25:00] Noah: i tried the TS snippet earlier and got a 401 until i set REDWOOD_API_KEY, then it worked. the error message could be clearer.
[25:12] Ethan: thanks, we'll file an issue to add a more actionable 401 message when api key missing or invalid, and include a link to quickstart docs in the error.
[25:25] Maya: for the pilot we want to evaluate both hosted sandbox and a dedicated small pool. timeline: pilot start next week, four week duration, then a decision.
[25:33] Sofia: sounds good — we typically do a 2–4 week pilot with crash-monitoring and one throughput benchmark day. i'll send a proposed schedule.
[25:44] Liam: security review — expected artifacts: SOC 2 report, penetration test summary, KMS integration guide, network diagram, and data flow.
[25:52] Sofia: we'll attach those. Ethan, can you drop the security checklist link now?
[25:58] Ethan: posted in chat: https://rbwd.co/sec-check, includes the docs we mentioned.
[26:10] [30:30] (Ethan walks through the Optimize suggestions UI, clicks into a sample eval report)
[30:45] Ethan: here's the regression table — if a change causes a drop beyond threshold, we mark it and optionally rollback. you can wire it into your CI to block promotion.
[30:58] Maya: good — that's a hard requirement for us.
[31:05] Ethan: quick note on SDK versions — we support pinned minor versions; if you need long-term stability we'll recommend pinning to a minor and schedule patch rollouts via our Console.
[31:20] Noah: are there pre-built integrations with our observability stack? we use Datadog.
[31:26] Sofia: yes, we have a Datadog integration for tracing and one for metrics. I'll include the dashboard JSON in the repo.
[31:34] [40:00] (discussion about pilot metrics and success criteria)
[40:10] Maya: success criteria: p95 <400ms, cost per summary < $0.10, zero PII leakage in logs, and SOC 2 evidence on file.
[40:22] Sofia: noted. we'll tailor the pilot to those targets.
[40:30] Liam: one more — what about bringing the model in-house later? is on-prem package available?
[40:36] Ethan: yes we offer Private deployments with on-prem option for regulated customers; onboarding timeline is longer (typically 6–10 weeks) and we do a pre-audit.
[40:48] Maya: okay that aligns.
[41:00] [48:00] (wrap up)
[48:05] Sofia: quick recap — we'll send the quickstart repo, docker examples, security docs, list of hostnames, and the sandbox key. Ethan will send the benchmark script. Maya will confirm pilot scope.
[48:20] Maya: thanks, i appreciate the practical walkthrough.
[48:25] Noah: thanks all.
[48:28] Liam: thanks. we'll review and get back with the security doc questions.
[48:35] Sofia: great, i'll email notes and proposed times for the kickoff.
[48:44] (call ends)
file_notes: Sandbox key to be provisioned; customer requested SOC2 + KMS docs. Recorded by Fireflies. Transcript contains occasional misheard acronyms (K-V cash for KV cache) and minor speaker attribution noise.
